targetQuery: unit testing fundamentals C# / xUnit arrange act assert
comparedAgainst: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/testing/unit-testing-csharp-with-xunit — Microsoft Learn's own xUnit tutorial, the top-ranking page for this query. Fetched: 977 words, TDD-flavored PrimeService walkthrough. It *describes* every run result in prose ("The test fails because IsPrime hasn't been implemented", "Run dotnet test, and two of the tests fail") and never shows a single line of captured runner output, red or green. No naming-convention section, no boundary-value reasoning, no brittle-test discussion, no exercises, no statement of what a passing test does and does not prove. This article is clearly deeper and is the only one of the compared pages that shows real, reproduced failure output.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/testing/unit-testing-best-practices — Microsoft Learn, 3,121 words, the page this article cites three times. Fetched and checked clause by clause against every claim the article attributes to it (see justification). It is stronger than this article on breadth of practices (magic strings, helper methods vs. Setup/Teardown, seams, private methods) but contains zero executed output and zero exercises, and never addresses the epistemic question ("what does green actually prove?") that this article opens with.

https://xunit.net/docs/getting-started/v3/getting-started — xUnit.net's own v3 getting-started page. Fetched: confirmed verbatim "Facts are tests which are always true. They test invariant conditions.", "Theories are only true for a particular set of data." and "Each theory with its data set is a separate test." Reference material only — no discussion of naming, brittleness or boundary selection.

https://martinfowler.com/bliki/UnitTest.html — Fowler's definition page, fetched as a sanity check on the article's framing of what a unit test is for. Fowler stresses rapid feedback ("should I accidentally break something, I want to know right away") and explicitly declines to claim unit tests prove system correctness; the article's narrower framing is consistent with him and, unlike him, is backed by executed evidence.
https://github.com/xunit/assert.xunit/blob/main/EqualityAsserts.cs — fetched the real source of Assert.Equal(double, double, int) to check the precision-overload claim (see justification).
justification:
I ran `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/testing/unit-testing-fundamentals.md` from PowerShell three times: PASS, blocks=16, executed=7, identically every time. I then went further than the tool and wrote my own capture harness (scratchpad) that extracts the seven `csharp run` blocks, writes them to `<id>.cs` and runs `dotnet run` exactly as run-code.mjs does, saving raw stdout/stderr per block per iteration, and ran that three more times. Diffing the three captures line by line: **the only line that differs anywhere, in any block, is the `Time:` value in the TEST EXECUTION SUMMARY** (e.g. 0.193s / 0.212s / 0.226s for `grades`). Everything else is byte-identical across runs, including the version banner (`xUnit.net v3 In-Process Runner v1.1.0+7ad077d852 (64-bit .NET 10.0.12)`), the per-block `Total`/`Errors`/`Failed`/`Skipped`/`Not Run` counts, the FAIL headers, the assertion diffs (including the `↓ (pos 4)` / `↑ (pos 4)` caret lines and their exact column), and all three stack-trace lines. Exit codes are stable and correct: 0 for the five normal blocks, 1 for the two `fails` blocks. So the wildcarding is adequate but *over*-generous rather than under-generous: the banner is wildcarded for portability though it is in fact stable on this machine, `Time:` genuinely needs it, and the stack-trace lines genuinely need it (they contain the temp file path `boundary-bug.cs(25,0)`). The assembly-name-equals-block-id property that all seven output blocks depend on (`Discovering: grades`, `Discovering: boundary-bug`, …) is real and stable, and comes from run-code.mjs writing each block to `<id>.cs` and `dotnet run` naming the file-based app's assembly after the file. `Total: 10 = 2 [Fact] + 8 [Theory] rows` is exactly what the runner printed. No flakiness of any kind; the new xUnit support in the harness held up cleanly under six independent executions.

I then re-derived every behavioral claim with my own probe program rather than trusting the prose. **The boundary bug is genuinely real, not staged.** Running the article's buggy switch against fourteen values: 90→'B' (fixed: 'A'), 80→'C' (fixed: 'B'), 70→'D' (fixed: 'C'), 60→'F' (fixed: 'D'); 100, 95, 89.9, 85, 75, 65, 59.99, 59.9, 55 and 0 are classified identically by both versions. That confirms every sentence of the solution: exactly-90 is graded one letter too low, 95 and 85 sit safely inside their bands, and each of 90/80/70/60 falls through to the next branch. It also confirms the later claim that a theory of round numbers only (95, 85, 75…) would have passed against the buggy version. **The brittle-test narrative is also genuinely real, not staged.** `[70, 80, 100].Average()` is 83.33333333333333; with `F2` the record's `ToString()` is exactly `"83.33 (B)"` (test green), with `F1` it is exactly `"83.3 (B)"` (test red, at position 4, exactly as shown), and the rewritten test survives both because `Math.Round(83.33333333333333, 2) == Math.Round(83.33, 2)` is true while `83.33333333333333 == 83.33` is false. The `summarize-after` block's `Total: 2, Failed: 1` plus the named failing method is real evidence that the properties test passed against the same F1 code, so the claim is earned rather than asserted. The 'prove it' gap is real too: `[-10, 50, 90].Average()` is 43.333333333333336, rounds to 43.33, nothing throws or clamps; I also checked the unstated other half (`[500, 50].Average()` = 275 → 'A'), so the no-validation point is if anything understated.

Every citation checks out against the fetched primary source. Bill Wake's page says, in his own words, "I (Bill Wake) observed and named the pattern in 2001" — the article's "named and popularized this as 'Arrange, Act, Assert' in 2001" is accurate (the page itself is dated April 26, 2011, which is the restatement, and the article cites the claim, not the page date). Microsoft Learn's naming section is verbatim three parts: "Name of the method being tested", "Scenario under which the method is being tested", "Expected behavior when the scenario is invoked" — represented exactly. "Protection against regression" is a real heading on that page and means what the article says it means. The AAA section does say the pattern "helps to reduce the opportunity for assertions to intermix with code in the Act task", which the article renders with brackets. xUnit's own docs contain "Each theory with its data set is a separate test." verbatim. `EqualityAsserts.cs` really does `Math.Round(expected, precision)` and `Math.Round(actual, precision)` and compares the rounded values, with the XML doc "The values are rounded before comparison" — so the article's description of the rounding behavior is correct. The toolchain sentence is accurate to the digit: `dotnet --info` reports SDK 10.0.401, OS 10.0.22631, RID win-x64.

What keeps this off a pass is one demonstrable factual error and one substantive technical hole. The error: the find-the-bug exercise opens "One character is wrong in `LetterGrade` below" (and the lead-in says "with one change to the production code"), but four characters are wrong — the switch has four `>` operators that must each become `>=`, which the article's own solution states outright ("Every `>` in the switch should be `>=`"). The article contradicts itself in the space of fifty lines, and a reader who takes the setup literally will hunt for a single missing `=`. Per this project's rubric a single factual error caps the technical score at 7. The hole: `GradeCalculator.Average`'s empty-array guard is not load-bearing, and the article's prose about it is misleading. I verified that `((int[])[]).Average()` throws `InvalidOperationException: Sequence contains no elements` on its own — LINQ never returns `NaN` for an empty `int` sequence — so (a) the parenthetical "throwing rather than returning `NaN` on an empty set, the 'divide by zero' case" describes a choice this implementation never faced, and (b) `Average_EmptyArray_ThrowsInvalidOperationException` passes byte-identically with the `if (scores.Length == 0) throw` block deleted, because it asserts only the exception type and never the custom message "cannot average zero scores". In an article whose entire thesis is that a green test proves one narrow fact and nothing more, shipping a green test that proves nothing about the code it appears to be testing is the sharpest thing a strong student could find, and it is left unremarked. Fixing both is small work and the article is otherwise the best page on this query I compared it against — the differentiation claim holds up: it is the only one of the four that shows captured red output, the only one that picks its `InlineData` rows by boundary argument and then proves the argument with a real failure, and the only one that demonstrates brittleness with a before/after that actually ran.

issues.location: ::::exercise[Find the bug], the sentence "One character is wrong in `LetterGrade` below, and one of the three theory cases catches it." (and the lead-in above it, "The next test class has the same boundaries as `LetterGrade` above, with one change to the production code.")
issues.problem: Factual error, and one the article contradicts itself on. Four characters are wrong, not one: the `boundary-bug` switch uses `> 90`, `> 80`, `> 70` and `> 60`, so four `=` characters are missing. The article's own solution says so explicitly — "Every `>` in the switch should be `>=`" — and I confirmed by running both switches that all four boundaries are misclassified (90→'B', 80→'C', 70→'D', 60→'F'). Only the 90 boundary is *caught*, because the theory has no row on the other three boundaries; that is a statement about the test data, not about how many characters are wrong in the code. A reader who follows the instruction literally will look for a single missing `=` and then be confused by a solution that changes four.
issues.fixLooksLike: Say what is actually true and keep the exercise's shape: "One operator is wrong throughout `LetterGrade` below — every comparison is strict where it should be inclusive — and only one of the three theory cases catches it." Or, if you want the 'one character' framing (it is a nice hook), make it true by breaking exactly one boundary: leave `>= 80`, `>= 70`, `>= 60` intact and change only the A boundary to `> 90`. That version is a genuine one-character bug, still fails only on the `(90, 'A')` row, and makes the solution's reasoning about boundary rows *sharper*, because the reader can then see that the other three boundaries are untested and would have hidden the same mistake.

issues.location: "A first test, run for real", the sentence "`Average` takes a set of numeric scores and averages them (throwing rather than returning `NaN` on an empty set, the "divide by zero" case)", and the `Average_EmptyArray_ThrowsInvalidOperationException` test in the `grades` block
issues.problem: The guard is not load-bearing and the prose misdescribes it. I ran it: `((int[])[]).Average()` throws `InvalidOperationException` with the message "Sequence contains no elements" all by itself — `Enumerable.Average(IEnumerable<int>)` never returns `NaN` for an empty sequence, so "throwing rather than returning NaN" names an alternative this implementation never had. Worse for the article's thesis: because the test asserts only `Assert.Throws<InvalidOperationException>` and never the custom message "cannot average zero scores", deleting the entire `if (scores.Length == 0) throw ...` block leaves the test green. This is exactly the failure mode the article is about (a passing test that proves a narrower fact than the reader assumes), sitting unremarked inside the article's own flagship example.
issues.fixLooksLike: Two options, either of which turns the weakness into a strength. (1) Make the guard observable and assert it: keep the throw, and assert the message — `var ex = Assert.Throws<InvalidOperationException>(() => GradeCalculator.Average(scores)); Assert.Equal("cannot average zero scores", ex.Message);` — and change the prose to say the guard exists to replace LINQ's generic "Sequence contains no elements" with a domain message, which is a real and defensible reason. (2) Drop the guard and let LINQ throw, and say so: "an empty array throws before the article's code gets a say — `Enumerable.Average` refuses an empty sequence rather than producing a number." Either way, delete the `NaN` / "divide by zero" parenthetical, which is not what this code does. Option (1) is the better fit, and the article could even note in one sentence that the type-only assertion would still pass with the guard removed — a second, free instance of its own central point.

issues.location: "What a unit test proves — and what it doesn't", first paragraph: A `[Fact]` is "a test which is always true," testing an "invariant condition"
issues.problem: Both fragments are inside quotation marks but neither is what the source says. xUnit's page reads "Facts are tests which are always true. They test invariant conditions." (plural in both places). The meaning is unchanged, but the article elsewhere quotes its sources verbatim, and a reader who clicks through to check will not find these strings. The brief's sourcing rule is strict enough that quoted text should be exact.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either quote it as written — xUnit's docs say facts "are tests which are always true" and "test invariant conditions" — or drop the quotation marks and paraphrase, keeping the citation.

issues.location: "One method, many inputs: Theory and InlineData", the sentence "Each `InlineData` row is picked to sit next to a boundary, not just inside a band: `89.9` next to `90`, `59.9` next to `60`."
issues.problem: Overstated — `each` is not true of the eight rows shown. `[InlineData(100, 'A')]` and `[InlineData(0, 'F')]` sit comfortably inside their bands, not next to a boundary; they are range endpoints, which is a different (also good) reason to include them. The brief's own pilot lesson is that `every`/`only`/`always` get checked.
issues.fixLooksLike: Scope it and say what the two extra rows are for: "Most rows are picked to sit on or next to a boundary — `89.9` next to `90`, `59.9` next to `60`, and `90`, `80`, `70`, `60` exactly on them — with `100` and `0` covering the ends of the range."

issues.location: "A brittle test" section, the sentence describing `Assert.Equal(83.33, report.Average, 2)` as "the documented way to compare a `double` without hard-coding a floating-point value that may not be exactly representable"
issues.problem: The first half of the sentence is right (I fetched `EqualityAsserts.cs`: it really does `Math.Round(expected, precision)` and `Math.Round(actual, precision)` and compares the rounded values, and the XML doc says "The values are rounded before comparison"), but the trailing clause misstates why it helps. The test still hard-codes `83.33`, which is itself not exactly representable. What the overload buys you is that neither side has to be exact: the *computed* value is 83.33333333333333, and `83.33333333333333 == 83.33` is false while `Math.Round(83.33333333333333, 2) == Math.Round(83.33, 2)` is true — both of which I verified.
issues.fixLooksLike: "…rounds both sides to the given number of decimal places before comparing, so the test states the two decimals it cares about instead of demanding bit-exact equality with a computed `double` (`83.33333333333333` is not `83.33`, but rounded to two places they agree)."

issues.location: "What a unit test proves — and what it doesn't": "xUnit runs the one path your test builds and reports whether the one assertion on it held."
issues.problem: "the one assertion" is not a property of xUnit and the article contradicts it later: `Summarize_ThreeScores_ReturnsAverageAndGrade` carries two assertions, and `Assert.Throws` is both act and assert. One assertion per test is a style recommendation, not what the framework does.
issues.fixLooksLike: "…and reports whether the assertions on it held" — or keep the singular but make it explicitly about this test rather than about xUnit ("reports whether the single check this test makes held").

issues.location: Line 60, "Every program below ran against the .NET 10 SDK (10.0.401) on Windows 11, x64."
issues.problem: Placement is right (beside the first real code block, not the opening paragraph) and the facts are exactly correct — I confirmed `dotnet --info`: SDK 10.0.401, OS Version 10.0.22631, RID win-x64. Two small mismatches with the brief's lesson on this, though: the form "Every program below ran against…" is very close to the stamped provenance sentence the brief bans ("every block on this page was run with…"), and the brief asks for the toolchain "where measurements appear" including CPU class — but this article measures nothing (no timings anywhere), so there is no measurement for the sentence to anchor. As written it reads as a provenance stamp with no local job to do.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either tie it to something the reader will actually compare against — the runner banner in the output blocks — e.g. "The runner banner in the output below is real: these ran on the .NET 10 SDK (10.0.401), Windows 11 x64" — or cut the sentence, since the site states provenance globally and nothing here depends on the machine.

issues.location: ::::exercise[Find the bug], "Read only the test names and the failure — not the switch expression yet"
issues.problem: The instruction asks the reader not to look at something printed twelve lines above it, in the same visual block, with syntax highlighting. On a phone the switch and the failure output are both on screen within a scroll or two. The exercise is find-the-bug rather than predict-the-output so the brief's rule about hiding output panels does not strictly apply, but the ask is unenforceable as laid out.
issues.fixLooksLike: Move the buggy `csharp run` block inside `:::solution` and keep only the failure output under the question (the `fails` block and its output can both live in the solution, with the output repeated or moved). Or reframe the ask so it does not depend on the reader averting their eyes: "From the failure line alone — before checking it against the switch — which score is misclassified, and in which direction?"

issues.location: All seven ```text output``` blocks — the `Discovering:`/`Starting:` lines and the three bare `[...]` stack-trace lines in `boundary-bug` and `summarize-after`
issues.problem: Not a defect today — I verified across six independent executions that both are byte-stable — but this is the first article to couple its expected output to two implementation details, and the consumer should know. (1) `Discovering: grades` etc. is correct only because `tools/run-code.mjs` writes each block to `<id>.cs` and a file-based app takes its assembly name from the file; any change to that temp-filename scheme silently breaks all seven output blocks at once. (2) `outputMatches` requires equal line counts, so the three `[...]` lines pin the failure stack to exactly three frames. The real frames are one user frame plus two runtime frames (`System.Reflection.MethodBaseInvoker.InterpretedInvoke_Method` then `InvokeDirectByRefWithFewArgs` for the theory, `InvokeWithNoArgs` for the fact) — a .NET runtime servicing update that adds or removes a frame would fail this article and nothing else.
issues.fixLooksLike: Integrator's call, not the writer's: consider a multi-line wildcard in `run-code.mjs` (e.g. a line consisting only of `[......]` meaning 'one or more lines'), or a `stack` flag that truncates everything after `Stack Trace:` before comparing. Until then, note in `docs/SHELL_NOTES.md` that xUnit output blocks are frame-count-sensitive and that block ids are load-bearing for any article using the xUnit path.
